title: Mali's king is in Cairo
body: Mansa Musa, the king of Mali, is in Cairo on a pilgrimage, a holy journey to Mecca. His huge company is buying and selling in the markets. Jamil offers you a share in his cloth sales to them.

choices.label: Put money into Jamil's cloth
choices.hint: It costs 9 now and pays 16 in a season. He sells to the Malians. You share the profit.

choices.label: Buy two chests of gold now
choices.hint: Jamil's friend sells a chest for 90, a little under the 100 the market asks. Two chests are a venture on one price, so the sum is large.

choices.label: Watch from the street
choices.hint: Your partners like a steady house.

note: Al-Umari wrote that the people of Cairo made great profits from the Malians, and that the price of gold fell.

sources.at: pp. 269 to 273; al-Umari on the Malians in Cairo

title: The canal is filling
body: The Nile flood is filling the canal to Alexandria. Kamil owns a boat that sails with the flood, and he has room for goods. The sugar buyers at Alexandria are waiting.

choices.label: Buy four loads of sugar and ship them
choices.hint: Four loads cost 220 dinars, and the boat brings back 230 in two seasons. The first boats sell first, and other owners will grumble.

choices.label: Let this flood pass
choices.hint: Kamil will sail without you.

note: Al-Maqrizi wrote that ships loaded with crops, spices and sugar set sail when the Nile filled the Alexandria canal. That was from 25 July to 23 August.

sources.at: p. 150; al-Maqrizi on the Alexandria canal and the flood

title: Another market, a better price
body: Zubayda sells linen in another part of Cairo. She says shops there get more for linen than yours do. She offers to sell your next cloth in her market for a fee.

choices.label: Sell in her market
choices.hint: It costs 4 now and pays 9 in two seasons. Her fee is high. Your neighbours will see you go.

choices.label: Stay in your own market
choices.hint: No fee, and you gain 3 in two seasons. Your neighbours are glad.

note: Al-Maqrizi counted 54 markets in Cairo. Shops that sold the same goods stood together, which saved buyers time and the cost of carrying goods.

sources.at: Introduction n. 11, and Background n. 24; the count of markets, and shops of one trade standing together

title: Bread is dear
body: Bread has been dear in Cairo. The sultan ordered grain brought up from Syria and Palestine, and buyers crowd the markets. Bilal needs carts for the grain roads, and he asks if the house will lend two.

choices.label: Lend two carts for a fee
choices.hint: You earn 5 dinars. The street will talk, and the officers will remember.

choices.label: Give bread money to your street
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars. Your neighbours will remember.

choices.label: Keep your carts for your own goods
choices.hint: Nothing changes for the house.

note: In 1336 Cairo had one of its ten big food shortages. The sultan ordered grain to be brought in from Syria and Palestine. A historian of Cairo's grain prices reports this.

sources.at: p. 198 and notes 7 and 8; the sultan's order of 1336 (note 7, from Shoshan 1993, p. 61) and the list of ten shortages (note 8, from Sabra 2000, p. 168)

title: Another house asks about Yusuf
body: A friend warns you. The Mansur house is asking what you pay Yusuf. A big house can offer more than a small one. Yusuf has said nothing to you about it.

choices.label: Ask Yusuf if he is content
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars for the visit. He will tell you the truth.

choices.label: Raise his pay a little and tell him why
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars. Other agents will hear of it.

choices.label: Say nothing and watch
choices.hint: It costs nothing now. Partners like a steady house, though Yusuf may feel unseen.

note: A big Jewish merchant house of the 1020s and 1030s traded flax. It is said to have used a whole army of Jewish and Muslim agents. Two scholars report this from an earlier historian, Norman Stillman.

sources.at: p. 17; the whole army of agents, from Stillman, as they report it

title: Boats on the river
body: A letter comes from Dilshad, who buys goods for houses in Samarkand. He writes that the river is full of boats in spring. He can book a place on one for your next goods.

choices.label: Book a place now
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. Dilshad tells others that your house pays fast.

choices.label: Ask him to find a cheaper boat
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now. The boat is slow, and your buyers wait.

choices.label: Send the goods by road
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now. The road is safe, and your partners like that.

note: A Persian writer said in 1340 that the river at Samarkand carries many boats in spring. He also praised its grapes, apples and melons, but he copied from older books, so this may be older news.

title: No ship will sail
body: A courier comes from Aydhab. The king of the Beja is at war with the sultan's soldiers, and he has sunk the ships. No ship will cross the sea now.

choices.label: Turn back and sell what you brought
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now, a loss on the sale. Your goods come home safe, and partners like that.

choices.label: Wait at Aydhab for a ship
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now, for an inn. A ship may come, and foreign houses see that you stayed.

choices.label: Send the goods by Quseir
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now. The goods reach another port, and the court hears of it.

note: In 1326 Ibn Battuta found Aydhab's ships sunk by the Beja king, who was at war with the sultan's soldiers. He sold his food and went back to Qus.

title: Sleeping in the gardens
body: A letter comes from near Hormuz. The summer heat there is so great that people sleep in gardens in the country. The writer asks if your people should be sent somewhere cooler.

choices.label: Pay for a cooler lodging
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars now. Your people are glad, and they speak well of you.

choices.label: Bring your people home
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now, for the road home. The work there stops for now, and partners are not pleased.

choices.label: Do nothing
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Your people feel forgotten.

note: Marco Polo wrote that people at Hormuz slept in gardens in the summer heat. He meant the old town, before it moved to its island, so this is older evidence.

title: The gate is shut
body: A broker writes from Alexandria. A quarrel has broken out between Muslims and Christian traders. The chief of police sided with the traders and shut the Muslims out of the city gate. Goods of yours wait inside.

choices.label: Pay a second broker to stand guard
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. Foreign merchants remember who kept their goods safe.

choices.label: Hold the goods in Cairo
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Your buyers go elsewhere.

choices.label: Sell to a local dealer at a low price
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now, a loss on the sale. The dealer tells others you sell fast.

note: In 1327 a quarrel broke out in Alexandria between Muslims and Christian traders. The chief of police sided with the traders and shut the Muslims out of the city gate. Ibn Battuta heard of it at Mecca, so he did not see it.

title: Hand your gold to the mint
body: Coin has run short in Egypt. The sultan's finance chief, al-Nashw, commands every merchant and goldsmith to hand their gold to the mint. A clerk brings the order to your house.

choices.label: Hand it over for coin
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now. The court notes that you obey.

choices.label: Turn the gold into cloth first
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars now. A chest of gold becomes 2 lots of linen, worth about 90. You hold goods while coin is scarce, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Hide some of it
choices.hint: It costs nothing now and 10 dinars in two seasons, a fine if it is found. The court trusts you less.

note: In 1335 coin ran short in Egypt. The sultan's finance supervisor, al-Nashw, ordered merchants and goldsmiths to hand their gold to the mint.

title: No galleys this year
body: A letter from Venice says the pope has told Venetians not to trade with the sultan's lands. No Venetian galley will sail for Alexandria this year or the next.

choices.label: Buy pepper to send round the ban
choices.hint: It costs 240 dinars now for 2 lots of pepper. Greek merchants of Cyprus will carry it where Venetians may not go, and foreign houses think well of you.

choices.label: Sell a lot of pepper in Cairo
choices.hint: You sell 1 lot of pepper for 105 dinars, less than the usual 120 while no galleys come. Partners see you sell fast.

choices.label: Hold the pepper and wait
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now, for storage. If the ban lifts, you are ready.

note: In 1323 Venice, pressed by the pope, forbade its people to trade with the sultan's lands. Venetian ships stopped sailing straight to Egypt for about twenty years, though goods still reached Venetians by other hands.

title: The army is on the road
body: A carter from Aleppo says the road to the coast is full of the army's supply carts. The army is gathering for a raid.

choices.label: Wait for the road to clear
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Your goods sit at Aleppo while the army passes, and partners grow restless.

choices.label: Go round by the coast
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars now. The way is longer but safer, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Sell the goods at Aleppo
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now, a lower price. Partners like a quick sale.

note: After 1322 Aleppo was the army's base for raids on Armenia. Eight campaigns set out from there between 1334 and 1348, so roads were likely busy.

title: Spice goes by another road
body: A spice dealer tells you that the Indian spice caravans no longer pass Aleppo. They go north, to the port of Ayas.

choices.label: Send a man to Ayas
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now. The road is long, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Stay with the old route
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Your stock runs low, and partners notice.

choices.label: Buy pepper from the dealers of Cyprus
choices.hint: It costs 125 dinars now for 1 lot of pepper, 5 of it a middleman's cut. Partners like the ease.

note: One historian writes that after the Mongols took Baghdad, much Indian spice went north from Tabriz to Little Armenia. It passed by Aleppo and Antioch, from the 1260s on.

sources.at: p. 196 (a passage she quotes from Ashtor)

title: The ruler has died
body: A letter says the ruler of Tabriz has died, and he left no son. Rival lords may fight for the throne. Your people there ask what to do.

choices.label: Call your people home
choices.hint: It costs 2 dinars now. Your goods are safe, and your people are glad.

choices.label: Keep them there and send gifts to the new lords
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. The new lords are pleased, and the court hears of it.

choices.label: Sell the Tabriz stock fast
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now, a lower price. Partners like a quick sale.

note: Abu Said, the last strong Mongol ruler of Iran, died on 30 November 1335 with no living son. His wife was expecting a child, and it was a girl.

title: The ruler has been killed
body: A letter from the east says the ruler of the Tartars has been killed by his own brother. A caravan there is held up for fear of war and plunder.

choices.label: Pull your goods out
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. Your goods are out of danger, and partners are glad.

choices.label: Send a gift to the new ruler
choices.hint: It costs 8 dinars now. The ruler is pleased, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Wait
choices.hint: It costs nothing. If war comes, your goods are in danger.

note: In August 1338 a Spanish friar, Pascal, wrote from Almaliq that the Tartar ruler had been killed by his brother. Yule thinks he was the khan of Chagatai.
